content_voiceover: This diagram shows the very first step of coagulation, the initiation phase, occurring on a tissue factor bearing cell after vessel injury. Tissue factor, shown in orange, binds circulating factor seven a to form the extrinsic tenase complex. That complex, assembled on the phospholipid membrane, activates factor nine to nine a, which is released to diffuse away, and also activates factor ten to ten a, shown sitting on the membrane surface. Some of that ten a then diffuses to a nearby cell surface where it pairs with prothrombin, factor two, generating a small amount of thrombin, factor two a. At this stage there's no factor five a cofactor yet, so this initiation complex is inefficient, producing only trace amounts of thrombin. This tiny thrombin spark is nonetheless critical, because it will go on to activate the cofactors that drive the much larger propagation phase.
keypoints: Tissue factor plus factor seven a forms the extrinsic tenase complex
Extrinsic tenase activates factor nine to nine a and factor ten to ten a
Ten a alone with prothrombin generates only a small initial thrombin spark
This trace thrombin primes the amplification steps of propagation
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the extrinsic tenase, tissue factor plus seven a, activates both nine and ten. Ten a alone with prothrombin makes only a small amount of thrombin, since factor five a isn't on board yet. That trace thrombin is the spark that ignites the much bigger propagation phase.
